name: props-drilling
intent: Thread shared state explicitly down a tree or call chain so every consumer's dependency is visible in code, and recognise the relay through intermediates that never read it as the point where a scoped context or a smaller state scope must replace the chain.
problem: State owned far above the code that uses it - a theme, locale, current user, request id, tenant or feature flag - has to reach consumers several levels down. The intermediates must accept and forward props or parameters they never read, so every rename, reshape or relocation of the value forces edits along the whole chain, and it stops being obvious which layer owns, updates or may use the value.
context: Component trees (React, Vue, Svelte, Compose, SwiftUI, Blazor) and layered call graphs in any language where one value is needed by scattered deep consumers while its owner sits far above them. Applies whether or not the platform ships a scoped-consumption primitive, because the decision is between explicit relay and implicit scoping - not between languages.
benefits: Explicit data flow: every dependency a component or function consumes appears in its props or parameter list, so find-all-references, rename and type checking work across the whole chain.
No hidden ambient state: a component or class can be constructed and tested with plain values, without a provider being mounted somewhere above it.
Ownership stays at the nearest common ancestor of the consumers (single source of truth), and lifting state up makes the owner of each value unambiguous.
Refactors surface loudly: reshaping the relayed value breaks the build or the test at every level instead of silently mis-forwarding in one leaf.
Works everywhere without framework support - the same discipline applies in a React tree, a Compose hierarchy, a Qt widget tree or a plain Java or C call chain.
Cheap at shallow depth: one or two levels of props are simpler than introducing a provider, a scope object or a store.
tradeoffs: Interface inflation: intermediates accrete props they never read and become coupled to data they do not use (change amplification when that data changes).
Wide refactors: renaming or reshaping a relayed value touches every level of the chain; renaming it mid-chain makes it untraceable.
Over- and under-forwarding creep in after components move: stale props linger, and optional or defaulted values mask data that consumers actually require.
Unclear ownership in deep chains: it becomes hard to tell which layer owns, updates or may read the value, and debugging means walking the tree.
Wasted work: intermediate layers re-render or re-execute when a forwarded value changes even though they never use it.
Tree-shape coupling: moving a consumer to a different branch invalidates the chain even though nothing about the data changed.

participants.responsibility: Component, object or module that holds the value and decides when it changes; normally the nearest common ancestor of the consumers.
Layer that receives the value only in order to forward it to its children or callees and never reads it; its appearance is the smell this record detects.
Component or function that actually reads the value and re-renders or re-executes when it changes.
Optional boundary introduced by the remedy - framework context, scoped value binding, implicit/given scope, task-local binding - that makes the value available to a subtree without relay.
Optional store or container (Flux/Redux-style store, DI container, request scope object) that owns shared state so consumers subscribe to it directly instead of receiving it through layers.

use_cases: UI trees where theme, locale, current user, permissions or feature flags are owned near the root but needed by scattered leaves far below.
Component libraries and design systems whose public prop API must stay stable while applications push their own state through the library's components.
Layered request handling where request id, tenant, locale or the authenticated principal must reach deep services without appearing in every signature.
Widget hierarchies in desktop toolkits (Qt, GTK, WPF/MAUI, Compose Desktop) where a session or document object is needed by nested views.
Selection and form state in list or tree components where the owner sits several levels above the items that render the value.
Isolating a leaf in a unit test or a component explorer, where explicit props keep the component constructible without ambient setup.

React component trees where a deeply nested consumer would otherwise receive repeated props through components that do not use them; React's Context guidance makes the relay-versus-scope tradeoff explicit.
Vue component trees like the documented Footer-to-DeepChild chain, where provide/inject can replace a deep prop relay only when the dependency is genuinely shared by descendants.

Svelte component trees where a parent needs to expose a value to descendants without threading it through intermediate components; Svelte's context API is the scoped alternative, while explicit props keep isolated leaves easy to test.
avoid_when: The chain is one or two levels deep: passing the value directly is simpler than any scoped mechanism.
The value is needed by exactly one subtree: move the state into that subtree's least common ancestor (state colocation) instead of threading it from above.
The intermediates only need to place the consumer, not the data: pass children or elements (or a render prop) so the value never enters their API.
The value is genuinely wide and stable (theme, locale, design tokens) and the platform ships a scoped-context primitive: use it rather than threading through dozens of layers.
A store already owns the state and consumers can subscribe directly (Flux/Redux-style): re-threading it through props re-creates the coupling the store removed.
anti_patterns: "God props" barrels: threading one giant app-state object through every level so anything is reachable anywhere - explicit on paper, unstructured in practice.
Renaming a value mid-chain (on -> isOn -> checked) so no static search connects owner and consumer.
Using optional props, defaults or null-object fallbacks for data the consumer requires, turning a missing relay into silent runtime behaviour.
Pass-through wrappers that exist only to forward props, adding indirection without owning or using anything.
Over-correction: wrapping the whole application in providers for every value, replacing explicit props with ambient globals.
design_principles: Explicitness over implicitness: a dependency visible in the signature can be found, typed and tested.
Locality of state (least common ancestor): keep state as close as possible to its consumers; relay length is a design signal, not an implementation detail.
Interface segregation: a component's API should contain what it uses; forwarding data it ignores is accidental coupling.
Separation of ownership from consumption: the owner decides, the consumer reads, the relay should not exist.
Composition over data passing: pass the element or consumer instead of the data when only the placement is shared.
best_practices: Do not split a render body or method into more layers than reuse requires; deep chains mostly appear where components or methods were broken up prematurely.
Treat a newly added relay prop as a smell trigger: check whether the state can move closer or the consumer can be passed in, before adding a provider.
When values always travel together, group them into one immutable, narrowly named context object instead of widening every signature.
When a scoped mechanism is chosen, keep the provider scope tight, freeze the value, and fail loudly (throw or assert) when no provider is present instead of falling back to null.
Never rename a relayed value per level; use one name from owner to consumer.
When touching a chain, delete props whose consumer is gone - over-forwarding is the residue of moved components.
